title: Slipknot reveal world tour with Marilyn Manson as support act
description: Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act.The eight-piece group, known for perform
body: Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act.The eight-piece group, known for performing in masks, will be joined by the US rock musician during their shows at London's Wembley Stadium and multiple dates of the South American leg of the tour.Some fans have reacted angrily to the news and said they will not attend the shows over past sexual abuse accusations against the 57-year-old.Manson, real name Brian Warner, has always strongly denied any allegations against him.  Thousands of fans replied to an Instagram post featuring the line-up for the London gigs, which also includes metalcore band Hatebreed.While some posts expressed excitement at the support acts, many were critical of Manson's presence on the bill, describing it as "disappointing".Others, who described themselves as long-time Slipknot fans, said they would not buy tickets for the show in protest at his appearance.One wrote: "Would've loved to see this but there's literally nothing you could do to get my cash in Manson's pockets."Another added the announcement was "such a disappointment" and they would not be attending.However, others disagreed, with one pointing out the two acts have a "huge fanbase overlap" and describing Manson as a "perfect support act".Manson was publicly accused of abuse by actress Evan Rachel Wood, who was in a three-year relationship with the singer from 2007.Posting in 2021, she alleged he "horrifically abused" and "manipulated" her and said she had spoken out to warn others about "a dangerous man".Manson said the claims were "horrible distortions of reality" and his "intimate relationships had always been entirely consensual". Several other women came forward on social media at the time with similar statements accusing Manson of abuse.Wood featured in a 2022 documentary series, Phoenix Rising, which focused on her allegations against Manson.He sued Wood and another woman for defamation, accusing them of impersonating FBI agents and forging federal documents.A judge dismissed some of Manson's claims, and he eventually settled the case and agreed to pay Woods' legal fees in 2024. Last year, prosecutors in Los Angeles said they would not bring criminal charges against Manson, external after a four-year investigation into accusations of domestic abuse and sexual assault involving multiple women.The district attorney's office said the domestic abuse charges fell "outside of the statute of limitations" and it was unable to "prove charges of sexual assault beyond a reasonable doubt."BBC Newsbeat has approached Marilyn Manson's representatives and gig promoters Live Nation UK for a response.

schema.headline: Slipknot reveal world tour with Marilyn Manson as support act

title: Five men arrested in RAF Fairford incident released on police bail
description: Five men who were arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences near RAF Fairford are being released on police bail, counter-terror police have said.A m
body: Five men who were arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences near RAF Fairford are being released on police bail, counter-terror police have said.A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of Sunday morning.Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said officers were exploring "multiple lines of inquiry", including whether proxies or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state were involved.The five men are all UK nationals in their 20s from London.They were initially detained on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.Counter-terror police said they remained under investigation and their release was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others".Three of the men live in Westminster, one in Camden and another in Willesden, police said, and they are aged between 23 and 25. A farmer who called 999 to report the three white vans in the village of Whelford, which lies directly east of the base, told the BBC it was "pure luck" that she spotted them.The woman, who wished to remain anonymous, said she arrived home to find the driveway and road blocked and saw a "large group of hooded and masked men"."When they saw me they ran ahead of me - some into the field and some towards the neighbouring village of Kempsford. I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.She said that she called the Ministry of Defence police at RAF Fairford but received no answer. She then rang 999 at 01:36 BST and said "within 10 minutes the village was full of armed police"."I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she added. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said on Monday afternoon that the three "suspicious vehicles" had been "subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts".Officers were considering the incident "from every possible angle", including that "this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state", he added.Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting on Monday afternoon and urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts".The Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident, adding that these would "serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK".The embassy said Iran "reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives".The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".Speaking at the Oval Office on Monday, US President Donald Trump said he wouldn't have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released. "We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this. A large cordon remains in place near the base, while 85 households who were evacuated on Sunday have now been told by Gloucestershire Police that they can return home.But police have said a cordon will remain around the three vehicles.Gloucestershire Constabulary's Temporary Chief Constable Maggie Blyth said the last 48 hours had thrown "our usually quiet and peaceful communities under the spotlight of the international media".Airspace restrictions have also been put in place above the base - nobody can fly within a five mile (8km) zone encircling it without permission. Banned items include balloons, kites, parachutes and paragliders.

schema.headline: Five men arrested in RAF Fairford incident released on police bail

title: Iran court upholds flogging sentence for singer who performed without hijab
description: An appeals court in Iran has confirmed a sentence of 74 lashes handed to a prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab, lawyers say.Par
body: An appeals court in Iran has confirmed a sentence of 74 lashes handed to a prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab, lawyers say.Parastoo Ahmadi sang while wearing a sleeveless dress during a concert livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024, external. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.Iran's judiciary launched proceedings against the 29-year-old after the video went viral, gaining millions of views, saying the performance was "in violation of the country's legal and cultural regulations".In June, a criminal court in Qom reportedly found Ahmadi and eight members of her band and production team guilty of charges including "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material".In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.On Friday, the defendants' appeal was "rejected" by a higher court without a hearing, according to their lawyers."In our view, holding the concert was not a crime at all," one of the lawyers told the BBC. "The trial court imposed one of the harshest punishments for these charges, although fines and less severe penalties were also available.""The Court of Appeal, despite having the option of holding a hearing, did not hold a hearing and upheld the judgment. It appears that the main reason for issuing this judgment was to deter the recurrence of similar events."News of the initial sentence sparked widespread reaction among Iranians on social media."May these dark days come to an end, and may women regain the freedom to choose how they live and dress, and may artistic expression once again flourish in our precious homeland," exiled singer Googoosh wrote on Instagram at the time. Musician Hossein Alizadeh meanwhile said he was "willing to take 70 lashes in Parastoo Ahmadi's place".Human rights activists also condemned the sentence, with Amnesty International warning that "flogging constitutes cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violates the absolute prohibition on torture and other ill treatment".In January 2024, Kurdish-Iranian activist Roya Heshmati was flogged 74 times after being convicted of "violating public morals" over a photo on social media that showed her without the hijab.She said a female officer forcibly placed a scarf on her head at a prosecutor's office in Tehran before a male officer whipped her shoulders, back, hips and legs, according to Kurdish rights group Hengaw, external.Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.When discussing hijab enforcement earlier this month, conservative politician and Expediency Council member Gholamali Haddad‑Adel - who is also the father-in-law of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei - said that Iran's war with the US and Israel meant authorities "cannot engage on this front as much as we should for the time being".The war began at the end of February, only weeks after Iranian security forces had violently repressed another wave of mass protests sparked by the country's economic crisis, killing thousands of people.

schema.headline: Iran court upholds flogging sentence for singer who performed without hijab

title: Andy Burnham to unveil public body to invest in electricity grid
description: Andy Burnham is expected to announce a new government body to invest in Britain's electricity grid in his first party conference speech as Labour lead
body: Andy Burnham is expected to announce a new government body to invest in Britain's electricity grid in his first party conference speech as Labour leader on Tuesday.The prime minister will tell party activists in Liverpool that the new publicly owned company, branded Great British Grid, will speed up grid hook-ups by driving up competition for connection projects.He is expected to put the proposals at the heart of a new goal to bring UK energy costs in line with other nations in Europe within ten years.He has also promised to use the address to give details of how he intends to pay for the new NHS-style social care system for England he announced over the weekend.Burnham is expected to bill the creation of the GB Grid as the first significant move in his ambition to provide greater public control of utilities, which he put at the centre of his pitch for power over the summer.He is expected to say that faster connections to the electricity grid could help fix a "cost crisis" in energy that has proved "crippling for businesses".Full details of the new body are yet to be set out, but Labour said it would invest in and compete for transmission connection projects alongside the three private companies that currently own and manage the grid in Britain.The party said it would also make it easier for firms waiting to be connected to the grid to finance connection infrastructure themselves, with GB Grid supporting and potentially co-investing in projects alongside them.Labour has said that funding for the new body will be found within the existing budget of GB Energy, the public green investment company set up by Labour last year and which is now headquartered in Aberdeen.Burnham's speech will see him promise an "honest conversation" with voters about difficult subjects, alongside the overall message of "hope" that he has made the theme of the four-day gathering.He is expected to say that he initially wanted to "give the usual tub-thumping conference speech" but that "the patriot in me tells me something very different is needed".It comes ahead of a tricky Budget at the end of next month, where the room for manoeuvre facing the prime minister has been narrowed by recent rises to the cost of UK borrowing.Ahead of the speech, the prime minister has promised to reveal details of how he intends to fund his plans to provide free social care services to everyone in England.He has said he wants to put his his plans before voters at the next general election, which legally must be held by August 2029 at the latest, before aiming to roll out the new system from 2030.There has been speculation that in his efforts to free up future funding for his social care plans, the prime minister could signal his willingness to review the "triple lock" uprating policy for the state pension.The policy - under which pension payments rise annually by the highest of 2.5%, inflation, or average wage rises - is expected to add billions to the cost of pensions in future years because of the UK's ageing population.On Monday, Chancellor John Healey declined to guarantee the promise - which has featured in every Labour manifesto since 2015 - would feature in the party's blueprint for voters at the next election."The manifesto will be the manifesto at the time, I'm not going to do that now," he told BBC Radio 5 Live.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham to unveil public body to invest in electricity grid

title: Russia's foreign minister Sergey Lavrov questions UK's future
description: Russia's foreign minister has questioned the future of the UK, suggesting it looks uncertain with "the Celts" looking to hold independence referendums
body: Russia's foreign minister has questioned the future of the UK, suggesting it looks uncertain with "the Celts" looking to hold independence referendums.Sergey Lavrov made the comments at a youth conference where he said he did "not know what will become of the country called Great Britain", according to The Times, external. The comments come weeks after the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland declared "Westminster's time is coming to an end" and signed an agreement to say it had no right to "block democracy".In response to Lavrov's comments, Plaid Cymru said Wales' constitutional future was "a matter for the people of Wales", and "not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit".In the conference, Lavrov also suggested the west had too much influence in the UN Security Council, external - the five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the UK, and the US.According to The Times, he said: "The Celts — Wales, Ireland, Scotland — are now seeking to hold referenda. "We do not advocate the expulsion of any of the permanent members of the security council. Although, of course, the scale of the British Empire, when it first took its seat in the UN security council at the organisation's founding, has, naturally, diminished to the utmost degree."Ap Iorwerth said last weekend there was "no turning back" on the independence journey, as he became the first leader of Wales to attend a Yes Cymru march.In response to Lavrov's comments, a Plaid spokesman described Russia as an "existential threat to modern democracy"."Plaid Cymru believes firmly in the right of nations to determine their own future through democratic means. That applies to Wales, and it applies to Ukraine," the spokesman said, referring to Russia's full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.They said the memorandum with the SNP and Sinn Féin was about "strengthening democracy, cooperation, and standing up for the interests of our nations and communities"."Wales' constitutional future is a matter for the people of Wales, and it is not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit," the statement added.Stephen Gethins, the SNP's external affairs minister who had sanctions imposed on him by Russia, said: "The Scottish Government is committed to ensuring the people of Scotland have the democratic right to decide their constitutional future, just as we support the people of Ukraine and elsewhere in democratic Europe determining their future too." Sinn Féin has been asked to comment.

schema.headline: Russia's foreign minister Sergey Lavrov questions UK's future

title: Social care: Four ways to reform the system
description: Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options?ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondent, BBC VerifyUpdated 28 September 2026 14:58 BST
body: Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options?ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondent, BBC VerifyUpdated 28 September 2026 14:58 BSTPrime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants major reform of social care in England to create "a system that works on NHS principles" and where "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". "There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same", he told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg. The prime minister has asked Baroness Casey to conduct a review on the "best way of doing it" and she has been asked to report by April 2027.Casey will also look at how to pay for any reforms.BBC Verify has looked at four options for approaching social care reform and how much they could cost.1. Cap on lifetime care costsSome people face extremely high costs for care at the end of their life.It has been estimated that around one in seven people aged 65 and over face lifetime care costs of more than £100,000.One proposal is to cap these costs with the government picking up the bill above a certain cash threshold.In 2011 a commission headed by the economist Andrew Dilnot proposed a lifetime cap of £35,000.Dilnot estimated his proposed reforms would cost between £1.3bn and £2.2bn a year. The cost today would be higher due to inflation and the ageing population.The Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron, accepted Dilnot's recommendations.But after the 2015 general election, which delivered a Conservative majority, Cameron delayed the implementation of the cap to 2020 over what he said were pressures on the public finances.In 2017, when Theresa May was in No 10, the Conservatives' general election manifesto proposed a different way to reform social care.This would have included the value of an individual's home in the means test used to decide what state funding they could get for care in their own homes.It did not, initially, include any cap on lifetime care costs, with the manifesto saying this was more "equitable" than the Dilnot plan. The May plan was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents and eventually dropped.2. A more generous means testIn England people can currently qualify for local authority financial support in a residential care home if all their assets - including their home - are worth less than £23,250.This is known as a means test - where the level of financial support a person gets is based on the value of their assets and savings.Some have suggested this threshold should be raised significantly so that many more people would qualify for means-tested support.Boris Johnson's Conservative government in 2021 planned to raise the means test threshold to £100,000.The annual cost of Johnson's reforms would have been £1.8bn a year over three years - although this was expected to rise over time as more people qualified.The Johnson government planned a new Health and Social Care levy to pay for the package, but this was eventually scrapped by his Conservative successors as prime minister, because they wanted to keep taxes down.3. Free personal careAn alternative approach is to ensure that everyone who is eligible, based on their needs, should get state-funded personal care that is free at the point of use.This would be provided free regardless of an individual's means and whether it was received by an elderly person in their own house or a residential care home.Scotland has implemented such a system.However, it's important to note that personal care takes in things like helping frail elderly people wash and dress and go to the toilet.But it does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs which are subject to means testing.The Health Foundation think tank estimates that implementing a Scottish-style system in England would cost £7.5bn a year by 2036.Like Scotland, Japan and Germany have systems which base entitlement to personal social care mainly on people's care needs rather than their ability to pay.Japan and Germany though have a mandatory long-term care insurance system which is funded through contributions from workers and employers.Both countries also do not usually cover the full cost of personal care so individuals are responsible for some of the expenses.4. National care serviceSome have suggested that the government should set up a national care service in England, similar in ambition to the NHS.This would mean all personal care would be free at the point of use while establishing national standards and care entitlement criteria.The Health Foundation has estimated the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system in England would be around £19bn a year extra by 2036.When Andy Burnham was health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government in 2010 he produced a plan for a national care service.It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they'd died.But the idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents. The party lost the 2010 general election and its proposals went no further.In the 2024 general election Labour again proposed a "national care service" without providing details or how it would be funded.And after the election then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer effectively kicked the issue into the long grass by commissioning Louise Casey to investigate social care reform and report back in 2028.It's worth bearing in mind that the four approaches above are not mutually exclusive.Previous reform proposals have often combined more than one of them - such as a cap on lifetime costs and a more generous means test.How could it be paid for?Burnham told the BBC that any changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse".One option - suggested by former Labour Treasury minister Darren Jones - is to get rid of the triple lock on the state pension. This guarantees that the pension rises every year by whichever is the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%, to pay for a new system of social care.But the long-term revenues from such a move are uncertain, because the cost of the triple lock depends on the future volatility of the growth of earnings and prices.The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has estimated, external that keeping it in place could cost "anywhere between £5bn and £40bn per year."The Resolution Foundation think tank has estimated, external that scrapping the triple lock now and replacing it with a simple earnings link would save the government only around £650m a year by the end of the Parliament.That would be well below the estimated annual cost of most social care reform options.

schema.headline: Social care: Four ways to reform the system

title: Man City charges: CEO Ferran Soriano issues defiant message to European club bosses
description: Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano has issued a defiant message to the executives of other teams about the club being found guilty of a ma
body: Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano has issued a defiant message to the executives of other teams about the club being found guilty of a majority of Premier League charges, BBC Sport has been told.He was speaking at a board meeting of European Football Clubs (formerly the ECA) in Copenhagen before its general assembly on Tuesday.Soriano was said to have vowed to fight the charges and the process had a long way to run, reiterating what the club's chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said in a letter to fans.The Press Association reported Soriano told the executives "it's taken eight years to get here and it's going to take a lot more time", referring to the start of the Premier League's investigation in 2018.He then left the meeting without answering any questions from the media.The report added Manchester United's chief of international football relations Jean-Claude Blanc and Everton owner Dan Friedkin - there in his capacity as owner of Roma - were among those to attend.City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centering around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations.On Friday, it emerged they had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them.Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told City will appeal.Sanctions are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the top flight or a huge fine.The Premier League has declined to comment, while City released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality".Chairman Al Mubarak told supporters on Saturday he was confident the club would prove their innocence."The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began," he said."There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position."But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."

schema.headline: Man City charges: CEO Ferran Soriano issues defiant message to European club bosses

title: You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it
description: Figure caption, How much is in your savings account?ByCost of living correspondentIf buying your own home is the finishing line, then saving up the mo
body: Figure caption, How much is in your savings account?ByCost of living correspondentIf buying your own home is the finishing line, then saving up the money to get there is a marathon.The "Your First Home" scheme, announced on Saturday, aims to help first-time buyers in England get on the housing ladder with a small deposit.Currently a 5% deposit on the average UK house price of £272,000 plus moving costs and legal fees - will set you back about £16,850, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.That's daunting, but here are four ways that experts say you can at least make a start on saving for a deposit.1. Make saving like a billDepositing an amount you can afford into a regular savers account the day after you are paid is a good way to start, suggests Anna Bowes, savings expert at financial advisers The Private Office."It becomes like another bill, but one that you can benefit from in the future," she says.The type of account that's suitable depends on your circumstances.Some of the ones that pay the highest interest  are only accessible if you hold a current account with the provider, she says.Other considerations are whether you can lock the money away for longer, to receive a better savings rate.If you don't have a buffer of other savings, then experts say an easy access account gives you the chance to dip into the money to pay an unexpected bill.2. You could get £1,000 a year You can save up to £4,000 a year in a Lifetime Individual Savings Account (LISA) and the government guarantees a 25% bonus. So, if you put the full amount in then the government will add £1,000 a year. But there is a catch, that has left some people out of pocket. Money saved in a LISA can only be used to buy a first home up to the value of £450,000 - a threshold that has not changed since 2017. The only other time you can withdraw the money is after the age of 60 or in the exceptional case that you are terminally ill with less than 12 months to live.Withdrawal under any other circumstances means you get hit with a penalty - so you could get back less than you put in.Ministers are planning to replace the LISA with a new First Time Buyer ISA, but there are no clear details yet about how it will work.3. Start earlyThe earlier you start saving the more you can build up thanks to the magic of compound interest. In short, interest is added on a larger and larger pot as time goes by.Bowes says that saving £50 a month from the age of 20 would give you about £41,000 in 30 years' time when you hit 50, assuming interest of 5% is paid a year.Start 10 years later, and you'd need to save more than double - £101 a month - to have the same amount at the age of 50.Investing in stocks and shares is another option, but the value of investments can go down as well as up.4. Save lessAn increasing number of lenders are offering mortgage deals with little or no deposit required.David Hollingworth, from L&C, points to mortgages that have deposits starting from £5,000 and allow people to borrow up to 98% or 99% of the property purchase price.They might not always be the best option, and not everyone will be eligible.And, of course, some first-time buyers turn to their parents for help. Again that's not available to all, but a survey by the Nationwide Building Society suggests that more than half of parents who charge their adult children rent are putting some or all of the money towards helping their child save to buy their own home.Get in touchAre you trying to get on to the property ladder? Share your experience. Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it

title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
description: Figure caption, Watch: Correspondent takes cover as approaching drone interrupts reportByNawal Al-MaghafiSenior international investigations correspon
body: Figure caption, Watch: Correspondent takes cover as approaching drone interrupts reportByNawal Al-MaghafiSenior international investigations correspondentReporting fromTaiz, Yemen"This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack."The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away.Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed.It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz.Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war. We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close.Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting. It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire."Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, Ali has remained at home under mortar fire to look after his goatsHe told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals. "I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway."He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too.At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach."We shoot over them, but we can't pull them out," he said.Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled.The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region.Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions.Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha.We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based.About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side.As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle.We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city.Image source, Liam Weir/BBC NewsImage caption, An international coalition led by Saudi Arabia is providing Yemeni government forces with weaponsTaiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line."It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said.The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces.Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.Image source, Liam Weir/BBC NewsImage caption, Twelve-year-old Ghana was seriously injured by a mortar while herding goatsIn the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied.Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby.She lay unconscious, her head wrapped in bandages, her face swollen and bruised. Her family were waiting at her bedside to learn what life might be like if she wakes up.A doctor told me the injury had damaged her brain. "She will never be the same again," he said.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, The UN says 130,000 people have been displaced by fighting in Yemen so far this monthAbout 20km south of Taiz, at the al-Monig displacement camp, families who had fled Mokha and villages hit by fighting were arriving, among hundreds of tents.We were told that 200 families had arrived in the previous 10 days.Maryam Saleh, not her real name, had come a week earlier from Mokha with her husband and five children. The youngest is aged seven. Maryam sat weaving a hat to sell so she could buy food for the day."We walked barefoot and we didn't carry anything with us, just our children," she told me.Her nephew was killed by shrapnel from a mortar as they fled, she said. He had been walking behind her. She described clashes and sniping both ahead of and behind the family and said she then saw armed men on the mountain."We thought we were finished," she said. The children were screaming and crying, but the family kept walking, she added.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, Fatma Mohammed Saleh, who cannot walk, says she crawled for two days before being given a lift by a motorcyclistFatma Mohammed Saleh was lying on an empty rice sack outside another family's tent. She has a disability and cannot walk, and told me she had nowhere of her own to sleep: "I have nothing… no shelter, no mattress, no family. Nothing."Fatma said she had been with her two sons and their children when the fighting reached their village. But she was slowing them down so told them to take the children and run, she said.She spent the next two days crawling on her hands and knees, she said."I was crawling and the bullets are coming from here and the shells are there. And the bullets are here, and the shells are here. And above me it was like thunder. I was praying to God."A man on a motorbike then saw her and drove her to the camp, she said. She has not seen her family since.On 22 September, the UN refugee agency said more than 130,000 people had been displaced across Yemen so far this month, on top of 5.2 million already displaced by the civil war.It warned that another 100,000 could – like Fatma – be forced from their homes over the next three months.Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer

schema.headline: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control

title: Lithium-ion battery fire killed Bootle mum and three children
description: A house fire that killed a mother and her three children was caused by a lithium-ion battery.Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eigh
body: A house fire that killed a mother and her three children was caused by a lithium-ion battery.Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eight, and Prudence, seven, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of 22 September.Following an investigation with Merseyside Police, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service (MFRS) said the fire was caused by an electrical event linked to a lithium-ion battery, which are used in e-bikes and e-scooters.Kev Johnson, of MFRS, said: "This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire."Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property, at 03:45 BST.MFRS said four people "showing no signs of life" had been found in an upstairs bedroom.A man was taken to hospital suffering from burns.MFRS has not confirmed what the battery was being used for, but they are often found in e-bikes and e-scooters.The fire service said there had been 150 fires linked to lithium-ion batteries on Merseyside between April 2023 and August 2026, and five fatalities linked to the batteries.Johnson said: "We're urging people to follow the manufacturer's instructions - only using batteries and chargers which have been supplied with the vehicle or approved by the manufacturer, as anything else can pose a huge fire risk."It's also important to know and recognise the signs that your lithium-ion battery may be failing – if it is swelling, making unusual sounds, has a strong smell, is failing to charge, or is smoking, please stop using immediately."Paying tribute, Ms Brabin's relatives said she was a "devoted and loving mother who lived for her children".They said the family had been left "heartbroken" and their "unimaginable" loss would be "felt forever".They also said "our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure" and they were "devastated by the loss of Elisha, Leo, Ellis and Prudence"."They have all been taken from us far too soon," they added.Listen to the best of BBC Radio Merseyside on Sounds and follow BBC Merseyside on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external. You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230.

title: Thousands of illegal ghost plates on cars revealed by new cameras
description: Figure caption, Watch: What is a ghost plate?ByRahil SheikhBBC Panorama and India LathamThousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other veh
body: Figure caption, Watch: What is a ghost plate?ByRahil SheikhBBC Panorama and India LathamThousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal.These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones as well as to track criminals.Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor.We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved.Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks.The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it.The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition.Ghost Plates: Drivers Cheating the LawHow cloned and ghost number plates are leaving innocent motorists facing fines, debt collection threats and years of stress.Watch on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One (BBC Two in Northern Ireland) at 20:00 on Monday 28 September.These tactics include deliberately using false plates that clone the number of another vehicle - and so-called ghost plates, where special plastic is used to make all or part of the registration number unreadable by most motorway cameras.One of the main providers of ANPR technology, MAV Systems, has been testing a new camera capable of identifying and reading ghost plates.At one test site, just outside London near the Dartford Crossing, it has recorded an average of more than 1,000 of the ghost plates a day over several months.Two other sites have been running for almost two years. At one, near the M25, detections have risen from 1,000 a day to nearly 2,000 a day - while at the other, near the Eurotunnel at Folkestone, the system is flagging more than 400 a day.'It has broken us all'Sharon Gannon's son, Jason Wallis, died in a crash where hidden registration plates were involved. She believes being invisible to ANPR cameras emboldens drivers to take deadly risks.Wallis was killed in Buckinghamshire in 2023. He and his brother-in-law, Lewis Baker, had been riding their motorbikes at high speed when they both crashed into a car. The car driver was not hurt.Baker survived and was later jailed for 15 months for dangerous driving. In court, he admitted using a device to hide his number plate from public view. He also said he and Wallis had ridden at high speed more than 100 times."It has broken us all," Sharon Gannon says of the effect the crash has had on her family.In another case, from 2025, 81-year-old Graham Slinn was killed on a pedestrian crossing when a car with cloned plates hit him at high speed.Image caption, Graham Slinn was killed in a crash involving a driver using illegal platesThe 20-year-old driver, Cain Byrne, who was driving without a licence or insurance, had also inhaled nitrous oxide minutes before the collision. He was identified after police trawled through hours of CCTV footage. One camera even caught the moment he had put the illegal plates on his car.Byrne was jailed for 11 years and six months for causing death by dangerous driving, driving while disqualified and driving without insurance. The victim's daughter, Nicola Timmis, says cloned plates are like a "gateway drug" which allow drivers to take more dangerous risks."It seems like it's harmless, but then one thing leads to another, leads to another, and before you know it, it's somebody dead," she tells Panorama. "It is not a victimless crime."Ghost platesBoth cloned and ghost plates look like normal vehicle registration plates when viewed by the naked eye.In the case of cloned ones, at least two vehicles are on the road with the same letters and numbers - with only one of them being legal.Ghost plates, on the other hand, show correct details for the vehicle - but they are made up of reflective materials which are difficult or impossible for most ANPR cameras to read.Cloned and ghost plates undermine the police's ability to track organised criminals, says Tony Porter, a former senior counter-terrorism officer who has advised the government on surveillance cameras."The police need an effective ANPR system that doesn't have weaknesses [and] doesn't put the public at risk," he says.While passports have security features such as watermarks and electronic ID chips, Porter says, "we tolerate a £10 number plate with no security mechanism on it".In the UK, there are more than 34,000 businesses registered with the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) to supply number plates.Anyone can currently become a registered number-plate supplier by filling in a quick form and paying a one-off fee.Panorama secretly filmed at a market in Essex to find out how easy it is to buy a plate in breach of the rules.Two out of three businesses we approached there offered ghost plates which they said could help avoid cameras policing London's Ultra-Low Emission Zone (Ulez) cameras.One of them allowed us to buy a plate without asking for either ID or proof that we were allowed to use the registration - both of which are required by law.Image caption, In the UK it is easy to set up as a supplier of registered number platesInstead, we handed over £40 in cash and, eight minutes later, we had a brand new number plate. Buying a ghost plate is not illegal in itself, but it would be against the law to put it on a vehicle and drive with it.Just two number plate suppliers have been prosecuted and forcibly removed from the DVLA register since 2020, a Freedom of Information request by Panorama has discovered. Only six DVLA officers are tasked with inspecting and auditing the thousands of registered suppliers in the UK.The DVLA said in a statement that it was "cleaning up the register, strengthening compliance and enforcement" and that it continued to work closely with police and Trading Standards to "tackle suppliers who break the rules".Nothing ruled outTo witness the scale of the problem, Panorama joined the police and DVLA at a location on the edge of Birmingham and West Bromwich to see a roadside operation checking for illegal number plates and other issues.Not long after we arrived, officers stopped a van. Specialist infrared goggles - which see number plates the way ANPR cameras do - revealed it was displaying a ghost plate. The driver received a £100 fine but said he was unaware the plate was illegal.The police and DVLA then visited the plate supplier, where staff denied selling ghost plates. But, using the goggles to view the supplier's stock, Panorama identified two ghost plates displayed on a wall alongside several legal ones.Police also discovered the supplier kept ghost letters and numbers separately on a shelf, which they said suggested "some level of intent".Image caption, A police officer shows evidence of "ghost" numbers and letters stocked at this West Midlands garage  The supplier, which told Panorama it did not manufacture the letters it used to make plates, received a warning letter, although a prosecution is still being considered.Police forces want to see tighter licensing and regulation around who can issue a number plate, says Chief Constable Tim Forber, the UK's policing lead on ANPR."Not a week goes by where we don't see an example of someone on cloned plates involved in serious and organised crime," he adds.There is a problem that needs tackling and a more robust system may be needed, according to Justin Madders, the minister in charge of UK vehicle registration.He says the government recognises this and is creating a national centre to crack down on illegal number plates, bringing together police forces to share intelligence and trial new technologies to improve road safety, tackle organised crime and drivers attempting to dodge fines."I don't think we can rule anything in or out at this stage," he adds.Additional reporting by NJ ConveryGet our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?

title: Drumcree: Orange Order parade dispute continues as main players hold talks
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Orangemen have tried a number of times to walk their route down the Garvaghy RoadThe main parties involved in
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Orangemen have tried a number of times to walk their route down the Garvaghy RoadThe main parties involved in a parading dispute in Northern Ireland are still in a stalemate, following a day of political talks and heated exchanges at Stormont.Members of the Orange Order are still waiting to begin their permitted parade, which was due to take place on Sunday morning, and walk down the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown. Protesters blocked the road at the weekend and after meeting the Northern Ireland secretary, a representative of the road's residents said the Orange Order should focus on a different route.The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, was due to go ahead for the first time in 30 years after legal challenges.Since 1998, the Orange Order had been banned from completing its Drumcree march - and until this year had been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route by the Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate disputes.The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation, while the area where it wants to walk - specifically along the Garvaghy Road - is largely Catholic and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists.Image caption, At one point on Monday night a group of up to 400 people gathered along the Garvaghy RoadWhat's happening now?Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant, who hosted talks on Monday, said he was "grateful to all" who took part in the negotiations and that constructive dialogue was the route to a solution.A crowd of up to 400 people gathered on the Garvaghy Road at one point on Monday night.Traditional musicians set up stall in one of the gazebos, with those gathered joining the songs.Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, spoke to the crowd via loudspeaker telling them to stay on the footpaths.Meanwhile, 35 Orangemen remained at Drumcree church and there were only a handful of supporters.Police scaled back their operation with only two police cars and one Land Rover in place. The road was not blocked.Talks with secretary of stateSir Chris said talks had been "positive so far" and that there were many people acting "in good faith for a good outcome"."Through the mist maybe I can see what that might look like," he added.The two most senior members of Portadown Orange Order met Sir Chris at Hillsborough Castle  and described the hour-long talks as "constructive".Asked if they still intended to walk down the Garvaghy Road, district master Nigel Dawson said "the law needs to be applied".Democratic Unionist Party MP Carla Lockhart, who has been with the Orange Order members in Drumcree, called on police to ensure the parade can go ahead. She said "mob rule" cannot win.Breandán Mac Cionnaith also met the secretary of state and said the Orange Order should use their outward route to Drumcree Church as their return route, rather than the Garvaghy Road.Mac Cionnaith said he was agreeable to some form of mediation but did not trust the Orange Order.Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald said her party "remain concerned" for the community, that even though the march did not go ahead, they need to know they can "breathe easy again" and "that they don't have the threat of a march being forced through their neighbourhood".The protesters on the Garvaghy Road were joined by members of Sinn Féin and the Social Democratic Labour Party (SDLP) throughout the day on Sunday.Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O'Neill joined the protest, prompting the Democratic Unionist Party to accuse her of acting unlawfully.What happened earlier?Image source, ReutersImage caption, Residents of the Garvaghy Road on MondayJust before 04:00 BST, a group of Orangemen tried to begin their parade but three police Land Rovers blocked the route.They tried a number of times afterwards, but the police denied them permission.Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson welcomed the lack of violence over the weekend.He said they were unable to allow the Orange Order their "lawful right" to parade because of an "unlawful and unnotified protest"."Our assessment was that to remove, at one stage, an estimated 1,000 people from the Garvaghy Road, including women, children and older people would have required such a significant use of force that public safety would have been significantly jeopardised, people seriously hurt and disorder inevitable," he said."In all of those circumstances use of police force would have been disproportionate."Figure caption, Stalemate continues as Orange Order march is blockedThe Portadown district has called for the resignation of the Chief Constable, Jon Boutcher, and ACC Henderson.Liam Kelly, the chair of the Police Federation for Northern Ireland, said officers showed "incredible restraint and professionalism" and managed "a near-impossible situation".The actions of the chief constable and senior colleagues "were exemplary and certainly beyond reproach", he added.In a statement, the Grand Orange Lodge of Ireland said there were "major political questions" to be asked about the "illegal actions and subsequent repercussions" of a number of elected representatives.What happened on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday?Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Protesters spent more than a day along the Garvaghy Road, with the road blocked at a number of pointsProtesters started gathering on the Garvaghy Road in the early hours of Sunday and remained there until about midnight.For most of the day, police maintained a sterile zone between the two sides, while officers repeatedly called on protesters to disperse.Orangemen set off down the Drumcree Road a few times throughout the day before stopping and turning back. On Sunday evening, a large group of people joined the Orange Order, and police blocked the road with vehicles. The Orange Order was warned they were breaking the terms of the Parade Commission's determination by having more than 35 people here, but loyalist activists argued they had not asked for a crowd.Image caption, First Minister Michelle O'Neill urged protesters to "stay the course"Speaking in the Northern Ireland Assembly on Monday, First Minister Michelle O'Neill said she was proud to protest with the residents who "have suffered generations of sectarian domination, intimidation and violence"."May I invite all those within unionism into 2026? The days of unionist supremacy and domination are gone," she said. "We will not be going backwards. We are about the future."Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said there had been a "total abdication of leadership".The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) politician said: "When the situation called for calm heads, Michelle O'Neill called people on to the streets, joined them and called for them to stay there."When her obligations were to uphold the law, Michelle O'Neill not only broke the law but encouraged others to do so."What could it mean for the Stormont executive?DUP leader Gavin Robinson said he would refer assembly members and elected representatives who were at the Garvaghy Road protest to Stormont's standards commissioner.He stopped short of saying that the party would collapse the Northern Ireland institutions.SDLP leader Claire Hanna said collapsing the executive over the dispute would achieve nothing but "create a vacuum".She did not think she and her party colleagues broke the law by joining Garvaghy Road protest on Sunday.Alliance leader and Justice Minister Naomi Long said it was a very difficult situation for everyone involved and it was not helpful for people to be "issuing ultimatums" and "ratcheting up the tensions around it".Long added she "cannot say for sure that there is a resolution" and that she questioned "the wisdom of picking at this scab and unleashing this pain".The State of Us: Rules V RealityWhat are the rules around marching and policing?Independent assembly member and former justice minister Claire Sugden said power-sharing at Stormont was "very vulnerable" to collapse, but added that "we all lose" if it did.Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows said the protest might be non-violent but it was "still illegal".He said the police would have to investigate and that could mean "knocking the door of the first minister".Timothy Gaston, a Traditional Unionist Voice assembly member, said Stormont had been damaged "beyond repair" after events at the weekend and he had no confidence in the chief constable.The Taoiseach (Irish prime minister), Micheál Martin, said the Irish government remained "very, very concerned" about tensions in Drumcree and added there was an "obligation on everybody now to stand back and to mediate an outcome".Church leaders have appealed for a peaceful resolution. Catholic Archbishop of Armagh Eamon Martin and Church of Ireland Archbishop of Armagh John McDowell called for an "urgent" and inclusive initiative to resolve the crisis, stating: "Too much is at stake."Two schools in the area announced they would close on Monday because of the continuing situation, citing the safety and wellbeing of pupils, families and staff.How did we get here?The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident.However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas.The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree route, but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against the parade. The row sparked some of the most serious public disorder in Northern Ireland's history and was linked to several murders.The row reemerged after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission - the organisation formed during the Drumcree dispute to decide on contentious marches during Northern Ireland's parading season - was overturned.On Friday, following 28 years of unsuccessful applications, the commission decided the march could go ahead with restrictions in place.Rather than start at 13:00 on Sunday as intended, the commission said it could begin no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested.However that decision was challenged in several Belfast courts on Saturday, before finally being given the go ahead just hours before it was due to take place.The Drumcree dispute was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading issues during the 1990s, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders across Northern Ireland.In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision upheld until Friday.

schema.headline: Drumcree: Orange Order parade dispute continues as main players hold talks

title: Three dead, including child, in Channel crossing attempt
description: A 10-year-old child and two 30-year-old women have died after a small boat that was attempting to cross the English Channel got into difficulty off th
body: A 10-year-old child and two 30-year-old women have died after a small boat that was attempting to cross the English Channel got into difficulty off the northern coast of France, local authorities have said.Officials responded to a distress call from the boat, which was carrying 105 people, after it departed from the Blériot Plage in Sangatte on Monday morning.Three passengers were treated on board but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter, the French Maritime Prefecture of the Channel and the North Sea said.Pas-de-Calais prefecture said its initial findings suggested the deaths were caused by trampling but an investigation has been launched to determine the exact cause.Of the 102 other people on board, nine were treated by emergency services upon their arrival in the port of Calais, the prefecture said.François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, blamed the incident on smuggling networks, which he said expose vulnerable people, including children, to the deadly risks of crossings.The prefecture described the boat as a taxi-boat, which requires migrants to wade out onto the water to board.Three other people died after similar taxi-boat departures last week, French authorities said.Monday's deaths take the total number of migrants who have died so far this year to 20, according to Pas-de-Calais prefecture. For the same period last year, it said the number was 21.Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous journey from France to the UK every year. In doing so, they cross one of the most dangerous and busiest shipping lanes in the world.More people attempt the route in the summer months when the weather is warmer and when seas are calmer.The UK recorded the highest number of migrant arrivals so far this year on Wednesday - with a total of 781 arriving in 10 small boats, according to Home Office figures.Two boats also reached UK shores last week without being intercepted by UK authorities, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent.In July last year, France and the UK agreed on a "one in, one out" returns deal, which was designed as a deterrent to stop boats from crossing the Channel.The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.In August the UK government said it was making progress in tackling small boats, with the percentage who had made the journey in 2026 much lower than for the same period in 2025 but added it needed to "push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade".So far, 2026 has seen 18,609 people successfully make the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 had crossed in small boats.

schema.headline: Three dead, including child, in Channel crossing attempt

title: UK tries to stop Trump's diesel export ban
description: The UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential stoppage of diesel exports and has started preparing for a ban, Chancellor John Healey has tol
body: The UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential stoppage of diesel exports and has started preparing for a ban, Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News.Diesel prices in the UK reached a new high on Monday due to supply pressures springing from the US-Israel conflict with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.Fuel prices are rising globally and US President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports, stating at the weekend: "We're thinking about it very seriously."  Healey, who admitted that UK diesel prices are "extreme", said the government was in discussions with the US, adding: "We're also making the provision that we may need to and we have our own stocks in the UK." Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Healey said: "We work very closely with the Americans."In the end, we're also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it, which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran."The UK depends on the US for around a third of its diesel imports and a ban would send prices even higher.US sources suggest that Trump is considering a ban to attempt to bring down prices for domestic consumers ahead of the critical midterm elections.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.In the UK, the average price for a litre of diesel reached 199.33p on Monday, according to the  RAC motoring organisation, surpassing a previous high of 199.09p in June 2022 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.23p.Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge.The RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away".Healey said he was "very aware" of these cost of living pressures as he prepared what he called a "breathing space" Budget on 28 October.A freeze on fuel duty, first implemented by the Conservative government in 2022, is due to expire at the end of the year. Duty is scheduled to increase by 3p in January and a further 2p in March.  Healey said: "Fundamentally, what we need is a settlement in the Middle East. We need an easing of the pressure of costs on business, the costs on households and on ordinary families that we see at the pumps in the most extreme level today for diesel."

schema.headline: UK tries to stop Trump's diesel export ban
